prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability.

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my single-part position. After the chair's questions I would define the achievement narrowly: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which lets many neutral atoms be interrogated in parallel without a first-order light shift, and its realisation by Ye's group at the 10^-18 level, including the many-atom and dense-lattice regime. That is a datable invention with a stable interpretation, reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in many laboratories and checked in international clock comparisons, and it is already used for tests of constants, searches for new physics and relativistic geodesy. It is distinct from the 2005 prize (combs) and the 2012 prize (control of single ions). The citation worded around the lattice architecture and the 10^-18 regime answers the chair's first question: it does not cover optical clocks in general, and it leaves the ion-clock groups, Lemonde and Takamoto as contributors to a field the prize does not claim to close. Two names follow the concept and its decisive realisation without stretching.
statement.case_against: My reservations are unchanged and I do not think the round has removed them. The prize rests on a lineage already honoured twice, and a committee can fairly say that record precision is refinement and not a new phenomenon. The credit tail is real: Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, Derevianko, the Yb and Hg groups and Ye's JILA collaborators are unnamed, and the contest between the Katori and Ye groups over the 10^-18 regime is not something I can settle from the shortlist alone. The SI second has not been redefined. Finally, I am an atomic theorist and I know my comfort with this field may inflate how clean the case looks to me. The topological-insulator trio is a serious rival on conceptual breadth, and I would not call the choice between them obvious.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification, and argues that it is broad, mature and overdue.
responses.response: This round moved me on the topological ballot. The B045 trio, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, is more coherent than the B004 string I had listed, because it drops the quantum anomalous Hall strand that Xue represents and keeps the Z2 theory and its first observation together. I also accept that the 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and quantum Hall plateaux and does not make this a repeat. Where I still differ is the cost the chair's fourth question names: a citation limited to the quantum spin Hall effect leaves out the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that directed Molenkamp's experiment, Zhang cannot be credited now, and the 3D and ARPES strands are cut off. Wording can describe the discovery but it cannot repair the attribution. I therefore promote B045 to my first alternative, not any longer the second tier, and I would accept it if the committee judges the breadth argument decisive.

responses.point: Kroll supports B022 but has disclosed a research stay in John Hall's laboratory and says the committee may need to consider recusal on B022.
responses.response: I think Kroll's disclosure is handled correctly and does not weaken the B022 case on its merits. A past stay in Hall's laboratory is a lineage tie, not a collaboration with Katori or Ye, and the committee can treat it as a disclosed bias, as I treat my own closeness to atomic physics. The committee should still be able to see that his is one of four B022 first places and not give it extra weight, which is why I rest my own support on the reasons and not on the count. On his overlap point I agree that the 2005 and 2012 prizes are the strongest argument against the clocks, and I answer it with the citation: the prize is for the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime. Since his second choice, B030, is held back on maturity, I put it in my alternatives for the same reason I did not lead with it.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and treats the unsettled pairing mechanism as not disqualifying, while asking whether the three-person limit can fairly omit Cao, Fatemi and other groups.
responses.response: The prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald and the 2018 experiments are among the sharpest theory-then-experiment pairs on the list, and the credited trio is neat. My difficulty is the one he lists himself: the origin of the superconductivity and of several correlated phases is still disputed and the results depend on twist-angle disorder. For a prize I want the interpretation to be stable enough that a citation will not need revising, and the lattice-clock claim already meets that. I do not accept that the credit omission of Cao and Fatemi is the main problem, it is the weaker one. I move B030 into my alternatives, above circuit QED, since the chair notes it has the widest second-choice support, but I would not lead with it until the pairing question has narrowed.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B045 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, values the topological invariant as a robust statement independent of model, and asks whether a lattice-clock prize would be strengthened by the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree with his point about the robustness of a topological invariant, and it is what makes the topological case a real rival and not a matter of taste. On his question about the second, I do not think the redefinition should be a condition: the clocks already deliver measured results in constants tests and geodesy, and the redefinition would follow from them and not give them their standing. Where I would not follow him is in letting breadth decide by itself. A prize whose credit string omits the proposal that guided the decisive experiment, and a deceased theorist, carries a fairness cost that a prize for a clean two-person invention does not.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B045 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and names B022 as the cleaner two-person fallback if the allocation is judged too contested.
responses.response: I note that his fallback is my first choice, and I take that as evidence that the two groups are closer than the vote counts suggest. His argument that Mele belongs with Kane because the Z2 theory is their joint work is correct and is why I now name the three together under B045. His withdrawal from B039 on a Chalmers link is also appropriate, and together with the 2025 timing issue it leads me to drop circuit QED from my alternatives. I would answer his comment on contested allocation with the chair's seventh question: when two cases are both scientifically strong I prefer the one where the credit can be stated without a missing name, and that currently favours B022.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B022 but records two reservations, that a record in accuracy may be a better instrument and not a discovery about nature, and that the unnamed Yb and Hg groups are a credit tail.
responses.response: I share both reservations and I answer the first differently from her. I would not claim that lattice clocks reveal a new phenomenon. The invention is a way of removing the light-shift obstruction that limited trapped neutral atoms, and the statute allows an invention. On the credit tail, I would not add names to reach beyond three people, since Lemonde and Takamoto are not decisive to the concept in the way the two named are, but I take her point that the citation must be explicit that it does not honour all lattice-clock work. If the committee finds the Yb and Hg groups decisive, that is a reason to reopen the allocation and not to treat my pairing as a settled attribution.

uncertainties: How the contributions of Katori and Ye divide, given the contest over who first reached 10^-18 and the unnamed Lemonde, Takamoto, Yb and Hg groups, and whether a two-name credit survives that.
Whether the committee accepts an invention in metrology as a discovery or invention of sufficient novelty beyond the 2005 and 2012 lineage, and if so whether the narrow citation wording is enough.
Whether breadth of conceptual influence, as in B045, should outweigh clean attribution, given that B045 leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism in B030 will have settled in a few years, which would change my view of its maturity.
statement.conflict_note: I work in theoretical atomic physics and have documented collaborations with the Lund attosecond group and Anne L'Huillier, with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and with Reinhold Schuch and Paul Indelicato on highly charged ions. None of these is a documented tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name on B022, B045 or B030, so I see no recusal issue. My closeness to atomic and precision physics is a general disciplinary bias that colleagues should weigh. I note Kroll's Hall-laboratory disclosure and the Chalmers links raised by Johansson and Olsson, and I leave their handling to the chair.
